meta.title: Who really said "You can't convince a believer of anything; for their belief is not based on evidence, it's based on a deep seated need to believe"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Wikiquote lists this line under Misattributed for Carl Sagan. It is not in Contact (1985) or The Demon-Haunted World (1995), and no source has ever been given.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You can't convince a believer of anything; for their belief is not based on evidence, it's based on a deep seated need to believe'?
meta.ogDescription: No book, no page, no date. Wikiquote files this line under Misattributed for Carl Sagan — it is in neither Contact nor The Demon-Haunted World.

answer.label: Not Carl Sagan — no source in anything he wrote
answer.authorDates: Origin unidentified · no work, page, speech or date has ever been produced
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this sentence in its Misattributed section for Carl Sagan ↗, noting that it is “Sometimes attributed to Contact (1985), but the quote does not appear in that book,” and that it shows up credited to Sagan in Judson Poling’s 2003 study guide Do Science and the Bible Conflict? — but “without source.” We also searched the full text of The Demon-Haunted World (1995) on the Internet Archive ↗, the obvious place for a Sagan line about credulity, and found no instance of “convince a believer,” “need to believe” or “deep seated.” The thought is very much in Sagan’s register; the sentence is not documented anywhere in his work.

source.excerpt: You can’t convince a believer of anything; for their belief is not based on evidence, it’s based on a deep seated need to believe.
trail: 1985 — Contact, Sagan’s only novel, is published by Simon and Schuster (Wikipedia ↗). It is the book most often named as the source of this line. Wikiquote records ↗ that the quote does not appear in it.

1995 — Sagan publishes The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, an entire book about why people believe unevidenced things. Searching the full text on the Internet Archive ↗ returns nothing for “convince a believer,” “need to believe” or “deep seated.”

2003 — the line appears credited to Sagan, without any source, in Judson Poling’s Zondervan study guide Do Science and the Bible Conflict?, the print attribution flagged on Wikiquote’s Misattributed list ↗ (Google Books record ↗; the preview does not display the page text).

2022 — Cornell’s own Carl Sagan Institute publishes an essay on Sagan misattribution ↗, built around a different fake (“Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known”) and one diagnostic question: is it likelier that Sagan said something thousands of people cannot source, or that he never said it?
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to show, because there is no located source text. Every version of this line online is the same free-floating sentence, always with Sagan’s name and never with a citation — the classic signature of an attribution that was never checked.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this sentence. It has no identified author, no source work and no first publication, so there is nothing whose copyright term could be measured. Carl Sagan’s actual books — Contact (1985) and The Demon-Haunted World (1995) among them — are firmly in copyright, but neither contains this line.

author.name: Carl Sagan
author.heading: Carl Sagan
author.metaLine: 1934–1996 · American astronomer, planetary scientist & science communicator, Cornell University
author.bio: Carl Sagan was an American astronomer and planetary scientist at Cornell University, and the most effective science communicator of his generation — the presenter and co-writer of the 1980 television series Cosmos and the author of The Dragons of Eden, Pale Blue Dot and the novel Contact. His last major book, The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark (1995), is a sustained argument about why people believe unevidenced things and how to reason your way out. That book is exactly why this quote sticks to him — and exactly why its absence from it matters.

misattribution.heading: A skeptic’s line with nothing to check it against
misattribution.intro: This sentence has been hung on Carl Sagan for decades, in three different ways — a named book, an assumed book, and a bare byline. None of them survives a look.

items.why: Sagan’s only novel, published by Simon and Schuster (Wikipedia ↗), is the source most often cited. Wikiquote states flatly ↗ that the quote does not appear in that book.

The natural guess, since the whole book is about belief without evidence. But a search of the full text on the Internet Archive ↗ finds no “convince a believer,” no “need to believe” and no “deep seated” anywhere in it.

items.who: Judson Poling, Do Science and the Bible Conflict? (2003)
items.why: The print appearance Wikiquote flags ↗: a Zondervan small-group study guide that prints the line under Sagan’s name and gives no citation for it. A quote passed on without a source is not evidence of a source.

The thought — that argument cannot dislodge a belief argument never installed — is old and well documented. Quote Investigator traces it ↗ to Swift in 1721: “Reasoning will never make a Man correct an ill Opinion, which by Reasoning he never acquired.” That page does not mention Sagan at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest position: no work, no page, no speech, no date. Wikiquote classifies it as misattributed to Carl Sagan ↗, and nothing we could fetch contradicts that.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Sagan so well
lead: Fake quotes travel on plausibility, and this one is extremely plausible. Sagan spent the last decade of his life arguing that belief is often emotional infrastructure rather than a conclusion — and he said so in sentences he did write. In The Demon-Haunted World he describes hoaxers demonstrating on camera exactly how they made crop circles, and notes that believers were unimpressed and simply argued there were too many circles for two men with a board and a rope. That is the same observation, made concretely, with a source you can open.

The manufactured version is punchier, more absolute and more flattering to whoever is repeating it, which is precisely why it outran the real thing. It also gets the argument slightly wrong: Sagan’s point was that all of us, himself included, want to believe things — he wrote about how badly he wanted his dead parents to have gone somewhere — not that “believers” are a separate category of person immune to evidence. Attaching a sneer to a man who spent a career refusing to sneer is the real cost of the misattribution.
context.detailsSummary: The Cornell test, and the idea’s real ancestor
detailsBody: The Carl Sagan Institute at Cornell published an essay on this exact problem in July 2022, prompted by NASA Administrator Bill Nelson quoting a Sagan line at a James Webb Space Telescope event. The line — “Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known” — was written by Newsweek reporter Sharon Begley about Sagan, not by Sagan. The essay’s test is the one to apply here: when no one can produce a page number, the absence of a page number is the finding.

There is a genuine, documented lineage for the thought, and it is a great deal older than Sagan. Quote Investigator traces it to Jonathan Swift in 1721, and follows the familiar modern paraphrase — you cannot reason a man out of a thing he was never reasoned into — through the nineteenth century. If you want to quote the idea and be safe, quote Swift.
context.pull: Which is likelier — that Sagan said something thousands of people cannot source, or that he never said it at all?
